newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Portugal government, unions wide apart on wages.
newsitem.headline: Portugal government, unions wide apart on wages.

text.p: The Portuguese government and unions ended a round of talks on Monday with no accord in sight on public sector wages, the final piece in the official strategy to gain entry to the European Union's planned single currency.
The government raised its offer to the country's some 500,000 public sector employees to 2.8 percent from the 2.6 percent it had been proposing.

But leaders of two of the three union groups to meet the government on Monday immediately gave the thumbs down to the new offer and the third, the Communist-led Common Front, was certain to follow suit.

"It can only be a rejection," said Bettencourt Picanco of the Union of State Technical Staff (STE), about the formal stance his group would take after a meeting to review the governent offer on Tuesday.
The STE, which belongs to the Socialist-led General Workers' Union confederation, had been pressing for a wage rise of 4.1 percent for next year.

The minority Socialist government of Prime Minister Antonio Guterres has warned that there is little room for manoeuvre on wages if stiff single currency tests for the budget deficit and inflation next year were to be met.
Further talks were scheduled for December 17.
Economists say that the government, which in its 14 months in office has always opted for negotiation over confrontation on important issues, has little option but to take a tough line.

They say three percent would be the upper limit for the public sector, whose wage deals set the pace for increases throughout the economy, without jeopardising economic goals, particularly for inflation.
"The maximum that the government could accept would be three percent," said Isabel Costa of Banco Finantia in Lisbon.

The government, which has made Portugal's inclusion in the vanguard of countries launching Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) in 1999 its top policy priority, is already guaranteed parliamentary support for a deficit-cutting budget for 1997.
The budget, which should be approved by parliament this Wednesday or Thursday, sees a deficit of 2.9 percent of gross domestic product (GDP), inside the three percent EMU ceiling.

The Socialists are four seats short of a majority in parliament, but the plan became certain to pass after the largest opposition party, the Social Democrats, on Monday joined the small, right-wing Popular Party in agreeing to abstain.
However with a question mark still hanging over the country's performance on inflation, the government had no option but to dig in its heels over wages, economists said.
Price rises are running at just over three percent but the government needed to get the rate down to some 2.5 percent next year to be sure of passing the EMU test.
"The priority is to control inflation. I think the government will be tough," said Costa.
